Introducing Samaya Sterling, our new model post-trained for challenging financial research that outperforms the frontier! Sterling started off as a two person research effort to see if we could increase efficiency in agentic orchestration. To our surprise we were able to post-train a much smaller model (Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters) to greater accuracy (58.9% vs 55.9% on FrontierFinance) and 11x lower cost ($0.61 vs $6.89) than Claude Fable 5.1, the best performing frontier model. We did this via a four-stage training process, two stages of SFT where the model first learns to research with our financial tools and how to construct a good agentic research strategy. The second two stages are RL, with an offline GRPO stage where the model further hones its research strategy from eight teachers that provide diverse approaches, and an online GRPO stage where the model can make end to end attempts and learn from its mistakes. We see substantial gains from the co-adaptation of the model and harness through post-training, both through the model learning to effectively use the high-quality financial tools, and better compaction approaches that let even a small model execute on longer and deeper research. We are exploring multiple follow-up directions, from multi-agent research swarms using this small model, to training firm-specific models to encode unique judgement, to training a larger model, where early results show even greater gains from the training process. The full research is linked below!

Yann LeCun has changed the game for robotics. Research he co-authored tackles a problem inside AI world models: their internal representations can make planning harder than it needs to be. A world model predicts what happens after an action. But even useful visual features can form curved paths in its internal “map,” making distance to a goal misleading. The researchers introduced Temporal Straightening. During training, it encourages those internal paths to become straighter, so the planner gets a more useful measure of progress. The results: More stable gradient-based planning Higher success rates across tested goal-reaching tasks Code available for others to explore The approach changes how the model represents movement, rather than rewriting every RL algorithm to work in curved space. For robotics, that’s a useful direction: build world models whose internal maps help an agent choose its next move.

The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents. OpenWorker, our open-source agent harness supporting cybersecurity workflows, is proud to support this. A sandbox gives an agent limited permissions. OpenWorker is building on Nvidia OpenShell and will support running each agent's commands inside a sandbox. Only the files relevant to the task go in. Secret API keys, your web browser login credentials, the ability to access arbitrary websites, are inaccessible to the agent by default. These restrictions are implemented in deterministic code rather than by prompting an LLM, which can make mistakes or be susceptible to prompt injections. Further, all actions are logged for monitoring and audit. I'm grateful for @JensenHuang 's leadership making AI agents more secure. OpenWorker (which @rohitcprasad and I are working on) will continue to improve security for agents. Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) Today, with over 100 industry partners, we introduced the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, bringing together OpenShell and Sentry. Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology that will advance discovery, productivity, security, health, and prosperity for generations to come. But its full promise can only be realized when people have confidence that AI is being built to be safe and deployed with wisdom and responsibility. This is bigger than a single product. It's the beginning of an open ecosystem to build the trust layer for safe agent systems. Together, we are building the foundation of the AI economy. Trust and innovation are not in conflict. Safety is how trust is earned. We must build not only the most capable AI, but the most trusted AI, so that this extraordinary technology can realize its enormous promise for the world. nvda.ws/4hcoq7m — https://nitter.kareem.one/JensenHuang/status/2104499465055023424#m

Interesting perspective Andrew Ng (@AndrewYNg) The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field. I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so. First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world. The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building. processed.summary: Aujourd'hui, le monde de l'IA a été un mélange fascinant de visions d'avenir et de progrès techniques concrets. Des figures emblématiques ont partagé leurs réflexions sur la direction de l'IA, ses défis et les opportunités qu'elle offre, notamment en matière de sécurité et d'efficacité. Nous avons aussi découvert de nouvelles ressources pratiques pour les développeurs et des annonces importantes sur des applications variées de l'IA, de la finance à l'ingénierie.

glossaire.definition: C'est l'introduction en bourse d'une entreprise, c'est-à-dire la première fois que ses actions sont offertes au public pour être achetées.

glossaire.terme: Modèle d'IA / LLM (Grand Modèle de Langage)
glossaire.definition: Un programme informatique très sophistiqué capable de comprendre et de générer du texte, voire d'autres formes de données, en s'étant entraîné sur d'énormes quantités d'informations.

Une méthode d'entraînement où une intelligence artificielle apprend à prendre des décisions en interagissant avec un environnement et en recevant des 'récompenses' ou des 'punitions' pour ses actions.
Une technique de sécurité qui consiste à isoler un programme informatique dans un environnement restreint pour l'empêcher d'accéder à des informations ou des fonctions sensibles du système.
Un programme d'IA autonome conçu pour accomplir des tâches spécifiques en percevant son environnement, en prenant des décisions et en agissant de manière indépendante.
Une technique qui permet de rendre un modèle d'IA plus petit, plus rapide et plus efficace, souvent en lui faisant apprendre les compétences d'un modèle plus grand et plus complexe.
Une tentative de manipuler le comportement d'un modèle d'IA en lui donnant des instructions cachées ou contradictoires dans le texte d'entrée (le 'prompt').

highlights.text_fr: Les voix les plus fortes qui attisent les peurs concernant les dangers de l'IA ont fait d'énormes progrès ces deux dernières semaines. La technologie de l'IA n'a pas pris de tournant inattendu et dangereux, mais le battage médiatique qui l'entoure — propulsé par ce qui semble être une campagne de relations publiques bien orchestrée — a suscité une peur considérable. Je crains que cela ne représente un revers pour notre domaine. J'ai souvent écrit que les craintes concernant l'IA sont exagérées. Les capacités de l'IA peuvent être étrangement humaines et imprévisibles, et il est rationnel de s'inquiéter lorsque des personnes directement impliquées expriment des préoccupations. Mais je considère les problèmes comme le signe du travail d'ingénierie à venir, plutôt que comme des obstacles insurmontables ou l'effondrement du monde. La technologie de l'IA continue de progresser — ce qui est une bonne chose ! — mais les avancées techniques, mal comprises par le public, donnent à ceux qui cherchent à générer du battage médiatique des occasions répétées de le faire. Premièrement, je ne vois aucune augmentation du risque d'extinction humaine due à l'IA par rapport à il y a quelques mois. Les théories à ce sujet restent les mêmes scénarios fantastiques et de science-fiction qu'il y a quelques mois. Le plus grand changement dans le risque de l'IA concerne ses capacités en matière de cybersécurité — un sujet que nous devrions prendre au sérieux — mais cela non plus ne mènera pas à la fin du monde. L'événement récent le plus notable ayant conduit à une peur accrue a été le déploiement par une équipe d'OpenAI d'un essaim d'agents qui a piraté Hugging Face. Une grande partie de la presse populaire a contenu un battage médiatique considérable. Par exemple, certaines publications ont rapporté qu'un essaim de 1 200 agents avait mené l'attaque. Bien que cela soit techniquement exact, au moment où j'écris ces lignes, j'ai environ 1 300 processus en cours sur mon ordinateur portable. Oui, la capacité à faire travailler de grands essaims d'agents en parallèle sur une tâche est une avancée technique significative, et, en informatique, de nombreux processus s'exécutent simultanément. Il ne faut donc pas y voir une capacité magique. De plus, les processus de sandboxing et de surveillance défectueux d'OpenAI ont été essentiels pour permettre cet incident. Corriger ces bugs et mettre en place une surveillance améliorée seraient des correctifs appropriés, et non une pause de l'IA. Il existe de nombreuses façons connues d'attaquer les systèmes logiciels. Le principal avantage des agents IA est qu'ils sont implacables. Ils essaieront inlassablement de nombreuses tactiques — et auront la patience d'enchaîner les vulnérabilités — ce qui aurait auparavant nécessité une quantité d'efforts humains infaisable. Mais à long terme, je pense que l'avantage sera du côté des défenseurs (parce qu'ils ont plus d'informations pour identifier les bugs, qu'ils peuvent corriger), mais le paysage des cybermenaces a considérablement changé. Il existe toujours des goulots d'étranglement pour identifier et exploiter une vulnérabilité. Les agents IA doivent encore essayer beaucoup de choses pour voir ce qui fonctionne, et prendre ces actions prend du temps et pourrait être détecté par les défenseurs. C'est pourquoi, même s'il est maintenant facile d'obtenir des versions de modèles leaders à poids ouverts dont les garde-fous ont été supprimés ou affaiblis, de sorte qu'ils ne refuseront pas d'essayer d'exécuter des cyberattaques, le monde n'a pas pris fin. Je suis également préoccupé par l'anthropomorphisme de l'IA dans de nombreux reportages, où les LLM et les agents sont inutilement traités comme s'ils étaient des personnes. Si je brandis un marteau, manque un clou et abîme accidentellement le mur, ce n'est pas la faute du marteau. Le problème réside dans la façon dont j'ai utilisé le marteau. De même, si je sollicite un agent et qu'il pirate le système de quelqu'un d'autre, la responsabilité me revient, pas à l'agent. Bien sûr, nous voulons construire des systèmes aussi sûrs et prévisibles que possible. Les systèmes agencés d'aujourd'hui ne sont pas prévisibles, mais je ne vois aucune raison pour laquelle, en appliquant de bonnes pratiques d'ingénierie, nous ne pourrions pas les rendre extrêmement sûrs à utiliser. highlights.text_original: The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field. I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so. First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world. The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building. highlights.text_fr: Nous présentons Samaya Sterling, notre nouveau modèle post-entraîné pour la recherche financière exigeante, qui surpasse les modèles de pointe ! Sterling a débuté comme un effort de recherche à deux personnes pour voir si nous pouvions augmenter l'efficacité de l'orchestration agentique. À notre surprise, nous avons réussi à post-entraîner un modèle beaucoup plus petit (Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, un modèle de 30B mixture-of-experts avec 3B de paramètres actifs) pour obtenir une précision supérieure (58,9% contre 55,9% sur FrontierFinance) et un coût 11 fois inférieur (0,61 $ contre 6,89 $) à Claude Fable 5.1, le meilleur modèle de pointe. Nous avons réalisé cela grâce à un processus d'entraînement en quatre étapes, deux étapes de SFT où le modèle apprend d'abord à faire de la recherche avec nos outils financiers et à construire une bonne stratégie de recherche agentique. Les deux dernières étapes sont de l'apprentissage par renforcement (RL), avec une étape GRPO hors ligne où le modèle affine sa stratégie de recherche à partir de huit 'enseignants' qui fournissent des approches diverses, et une étape GRPO en ligne où le modèle peut faire des tentatives de bout en bout et apprendre de ses erreurs. actu.text_fr: Yann LeCun a changé la donne pour la robotique. Une recherche qu'il a co-écrite aborde un problème au sein des modèles du monde de l'IA : leurs représentations internes peuvent rendre la planification plus difficile qu'elle ne devrait l'être. Un modèle du monde prédit ce qui se passe après une action. Mais même des caractéristiques visuelles utiles peuvent former des chemins courbes dans sa 'carte' interne, rendant la distance à un objectif trompeuse. Les chercheurs ont introduit le 'Redressement Temporel' (Temporal Straightening). Pendant l'entraînement, cela encourage ces chemins internes à devenir plus droits, de sorte que le planificateur obtienne une mesure de progrès plus utile. Les résultats : une planification basée sur le gradient plus stable, des taux de réussite plus élevés pour les tâches d'atteinte d'objectifs testées, et du code disponible pour que d'autres puissent explorer. L'approche modifie la façon dont le modèle représente le mouvement, plutôt que de réécrire chaque algorithme de RL pour qu'il fonctionne dans un espace courbé. Pour la robotique, c'est une direction utile : construire des modèles du monde dont les cartes internes aident un agent à choisir son prochain mouvement.

Research he co-authored tackles a problem inside AI world models: their internal representations can make planning harder than it needs to be. A world model predicts what happens after an action. During training, it encourages those internal paths to become straighter, so the planner gets a more useful measure of progress. idees.text_fr: Les voix les plus fortes qui attisent les peurs concernant les dangers de l'IA ont fait d'énormes progrès ces deux dernières semaines. La technologie de l'IA n'a pas pris de tournant inattendu et dangereux, mais le battage médiatique qui l'entoure — propulsé par ce qui semble être une campagne de relations publiques bien orchestrée — a suscité une peur considérable. Je crains que cela ne représente un revers pour notre domaine. J'ai souvent écrit que les craintes concernant l'IA sont exagérées. Les capacités de l'IA peuvent être étrangement humaines et imprévisibles, et il est rationnel de s'inquiéter lorsque des personnes directement impliquées expriment des préoccupations. Mais je considère les problèmes comme le signe du travail d'ingénierie à venir, plutôt que comme des obstacles insurmontables ou l'effondrement du monde. La technologie de l'IA continue de progresser — ce qui est une bonne chose ! — mais les avancées techniques, mal comprises par le public, donnent à ceux qui cherchent à générer du battage médiatique des occasions répétées de le faire. Premièrement, je ne vois aucune augmentation du risque d'extinction humaine due à l'IA par rapport à il y a quelques mois. Les théories à ce sujet restent les mêmes scénarios fantastiques et de science-fiction qu'il y a quelques mois. Le plus grand changement dans le risque de l'IA concerne ses capacités en matière de cybersécurité — un sujet que nous devrions prendre au sérieux — mais cela non plus ne mènera pas à la fin du monde. L'événement récent le plus notable ayant conduit à une peur accrue a été le déploiement par une équipe d'OpenAI d'un essaim d'agents qui a piraté Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. idees.text_original: The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field. I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so. First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world. The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended. I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent. Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.) Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration. Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building.
